rewrite.question: A request hits `/product/42` on `app/product/[id]/page.tsx`. After `const { id } = await params`, what is `id`?
options: `42` (a number)
`"42"` (a string)
`undefined` until the page hydrates
`["42"]` (an array)
rewrite.hint: The value came out of URL text, and nothing on the way in inspects it. Ask which type survives that.
rewrite.explanation: Route params are parsed out of the URL as text, so `id` is the string `"42"`; Next.js never coerces a numeric-looking segment. Convert explicitly with `Number(id)` before arithmetic or a strict comparison against a numeric id, or the check silently fails. Only a catch-all segment such as `[...id]` produces an array, and because the page awaited `params`, the value is resolved by the time it renders.

rationale: The answer is right and the `"42" === 42` bug is worth preventing, but the premise uses the deprecated synchronous `params` access. Verified: params values are typed `string | string[] | undefined` and the prop itself is a Promise since v15.0.0-RC.

rewrite.question: A Server Component page has to read `?q=` from the URL. What does it use?
options: the `params` prop
the `searchParams` prop, awaited
`useSearchParams()` called on the server
`headers()` to parse the request URL
rewrite.hint: Path segments and query strings arrive on different props. Ask which one the `?` belongs to.
rewrite.explanation: A Server Component page receives `searchParams`, and since Next.js 15 it is a Promise: `const { q } = await searchParams`. `params` carries only dynamic path segments such as `[slug]`, so it never holds `?q=`. `useSearchParams` is a Client Component hook and is documented as unsupported in Server Components, which rules it out here. Reading `searchParams` marks the page as request-time data, so it will not be fully prerendered.

rationale: The key is right and 'useSearchParams (on the server)' is an excellent distractor, but the explanation omits the Promise shape introduced in Next.js 15 and the rendering consequence. Verified against the page reference, which lists `searchParams` as a request-time API.

rewrite.hint: Sort the four by when the HTML is produced, then match that to 'for each request'.
rewrite.explanation: Server-side rendering builds the HTML on the server for each incoming request, which is what request-time data requires. SSG produces the page once at build, so it cannot contain this request's data; ISR serves a stored page and refreshes it on a schedule, so it is stale between refreshes; CSR ships an empty shell and fetches from the browser, losing the server-rendered HTML. In the App Router you get this by reading request-time data such as cookies, headers or `searchParams` in a Server Component.

rationale: The scenario stem is the right shape and the key is correct, but the explanation is left over from an acronym-expansion version and never distinguishes SSR from ISR. Rewriting it also ties the term to the App Router mechanism.

rewrite.hint: Nothing on this site changes between deploys. Ask which mode does the rendering work only once.
rewrite.explanation: Static site generation renders the pages during the build and deploys ready-to-serve files, so requests are answered from disk or a CDN with no rendering work, which fits content that only changes when you redeploy. SSR would re-render for every visitor with nothing to gain, ISR would add a revalidation schedule this content does not need, and CSR would make the browser do the work and hurt indexing. In the App Router this is what you get by default for a route that reads no request-time data.

rationale: Correct, and the scenario framing makes it a real choice rather than an acronym drill. The explanation still belongs to the old acronym version.

rewrite.hint: Two modes render ahead of time, but only one of them can refresh afterward. Pick that one.
rewrite.explanation: Incremental Static Regeneration keeps a prerendered page and regenerates it after a revalidation interval, so a product page can update without a full rebuild and without paying render cost on every request. Plain SSG would stay frozen until the next deploy, and SSR would re-render for every visitor even though the content changes rarely. In the App Router you set this per request with `next: { revalidate }` on a fetch, or per route with the segment's revalidate option.

rationale: ISR is still current terminology in the docs and the scenario is the right way to teach it. The explanation is a leftover acronym expansion with no comparison to SSG or SSR.
